rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2.6 and Fig. 1 report new, previously unpublished bean-yield data from the authors' own FACE trial in Brazil (C. arabica cv. Catua<U+00ED>, three harvests 2013-2015, elevated vs ambient CO2, n = 10 <U+00B1> SE); the rest of the paper is a narrative review.
rows.notes: The study contains no evidence on drip or sensor-based irrigation. Its own data concern crop yield under elevated CO2 in a rain-fed, unirrigated FACE trial. Irrigation is mentioned only in passing: the authors speculate that positive CO2 effects may be more evident in intensive systems 'including irrigation', and cite Verhage et al. (2017) assuming irrigation use remains unchanged, and Vinecky et al. (2017) on water supply affecting bean quality; none of this is the study's own result on drip irrigation as a drought-adaptation measure. Q1 is marginal because the paper self-identifies as a review, but Fig. 1 is genuinely new own data.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2.6 and Fig. 1 report the authors' own new bean-yield data from a FACE trial in Brazil (three harvests, elevated vs ambient CO2, n = 10 <U+00B1> SE).
rows.notes: The study reports nothing on rainwater harvesting or micro-irrigation. Its own result is a ~28% mean yield increase under elevated CO2 in an unirrigated, rain-fed FACE trial, with yield depressed by a 2014 drought. Irrigation appears only as a passing speculation (CO2 benefits likely larger in intensive systems including irrigation) and in cited work (Verhage et al. 2017; Vinecky et al. 2017), which does not count as own evidence. Q1 marginal: self-described review with one new dataset.

notes: The paper is a narrative review on coffee physiology under elevated CO2 and warming that also presents one new dataset (FACE yield, Fig. 1). It contains no experiment, survey or model on drip, sensor-based or micro-irrigation, nor on rainwater harvesting; both claim rows are unsupported by the study's own evidence. Full text appears complete.
